title: Winter Dreams
subtitle: F. Scott Fitzgerald (1922) — a caddy who quits, a girl on a golf course, and the price of getting everything you wanted.
crosslink: Need an easier version? Read this story at A2/B1 level →
intention: you'll tell the story of a poor boy who becomes rich and loses the one thing money was for, and use the language of regret and hindsight — wish, if only, should have, needn't have — to look back the way Dexter does.
warmup: Think of something you wanted badly at fifteen. Did you get it? What did it feel like when you did — or didn't?
Is it better to want something you can never have, or to have it and stop wanting it?
What is the difference between ambition and greed? Where is the line?
vocab_intro: Before we read, let's unlock the words you'll need. Think first — the Reveal only confirms.

vocab.heading: A. Work it out from the sentence
vocab.instruction: Read each sentence aloud and say what the bold word means from the rest of the sentence. Then reveal.

items.sent: The empty golf course under snow filled him with a profound melancholy: nothing moved, nothing shone, and summer felt a hundred years away.
Playing the course as a guest, he felt like a trespasser — as if at any moment someone would ask what a caddy was doing on the members' side of the rope.
items.meaning: a trespasser (n) — someone who enters a place where they have no right to be. (v: to trespass)

items.sent: Her petulance at dinner unsettled him: a sulk over nothing, a sharp word about the chicken, a smile with no pleasure in it.
She beckoned him and yawned at him and beckoned him again: two years of small indignities that he swallowed because he could not stop loving her.
items.meaning: an indignity (n) — a humiliating treatment; something that wounds your dignity.

vocab.heading: B. Build the word
vocab.instruction: You know one form of the word. Say the form the sentence needs, then reveal.

items.sent: You know principle (a moral rule). What adjective, with 'un-', describes a person who has none — 'the most direct and ___ personality he had ever met'?
items.meaning: unprincipled (adj) — without moral principles; doing whatever you want. principle → principled → unprincipled

items.sent: You know vulnerable (easy to hurt). What adjective means the opposite — a man who has nothing left to lose thinks he is ___?
items.meaning: invulnerable (adj) — impossible to hurt or damage. vulnerable → invulnerable

items.sent: You know correct. What adjective, from the same root, means 'impossible to correct or improve' — 'the ___ lips of Judy Jones'?
items.meaning: incorrigible (adj) — impossible to correct or reform; hopelessly and permanently so. correct → incorrigible (same Latin root)

vocab.heading: C. Choose the meaning
vocab.instruction: One sentence, three options. Say a, b or c — then reveal.

items.sent: He wanted not the company of glittering people but the glittering things themselves. Glittering means: (a) shining brightly with many small flashes (b) very old (c) dangerous
items.meaning: (a) — glittering (adj) — shining with small bright flashes; figuratively, glamorous and impressive.

items.sent: Her kisses created not hunger but surfeit — and a surfeit that demanded more surfeit. Surfeit is: (a) a shortage (b) an excess, too much of something (c) a promise
items.meaning: (b) — surfeit (n) — an excessive amount, more than enough. A rare, literary word.

items.sent: No disappointment with her world could cure his illusion about her. An illusion is: (a) a true memory (b) a plan (c) a false belief or idea that seems real
items.meaning: (c) — an illusion (n) — a false idea or belief; something that seems real but is not. (v: disillusion)

vocab_use: Sort the ten words into Dexter, Judy and the world of the rich. Say why.
Using glittering, illusion and indignity, predict how a boy's winter dreams turn out.
story_intro: Fitzgerald's own text, cut hard — the original is three times this length. Read each part; after it, try the quick check from memory, then talk about the question.

story.title: Part 1 — The caddy who quit

paras.from: Some of the caddies were poor as sin
paras.to: dictated to by his winter dreams.
skip: In April the winter ceased abruptly
He became a golf champion and defeated
"I don't know what we're supposed to do now,"
"Boy, do you know where the golf teacher is?"
Dexter knew that there was something dismal about this Northern spring
She had come eagerly out on to the course
Dexter stood perfectly still, his mouth slightly ajar

check.q: Why does Dexter caddy at all, and what does he do with the long Minnesota winter?
check.a: Only for pocket-money — his father owns the second-best grocery store. In winter he skis over the buried golf course, filled with melancholy, and lives in his 'winter dreams' of triumph at the club.

check.q: What actually makes him quit, that morning, after Mr. Jones has begged him to stay?
check.a: An eleven-year-old girl, Judy Jones, arrives with her nurse and five new golf clubs, treats him as 'Boy', hits her club on the ground in a rage — and something in him is so shaken that he hands in his badge rather than carry her bag.

story.discuss: Fitzgerald says Dexter 'was unconsciously dictated to by his winter dreams'. What are winter dreams — and why does quitting a job he loves count as one?

story.title: Part 2 — Judy Jones

paras.from: He made money. It was rather amazing.
skip: It was a small laundry when he went into it
It was a curious day, slashed abruptly
not even a good golfer any more.
There was a fish jumping and a star shining and the lights around the lake were gleaming. Over on a dark peninsula
The nose of the boat bumped the raft
Then she was in the water, swimming
When the time had come for him to wear good clothes
But carelessness was for his children.
He remembered the last time he had seen her father
used as footstools by fashionable lakes.
During dinner she slipped into a moody depression
A lump rose in Dexter's throat
He did not consider it necessary to remark
Her glance fell casually on each of the men
Later in the afternoon the sun went down with a riotous swirl
Two white streamers of cleft water
They moved out into the lake
"Father and mother won't be here," she said thoughtfully.
"Perhaps he was afraid to tell you."
He might not object to widows, but----

check.q: How does Dexter make his money, and how does he come to be on the golf course as a guest at twenty-three?
check.a: He borrows a thousand dollars on his degree and 'his confident mouth', buys into a laundry, and specialises in washing rich men's golf stockings; by twenty-seven he owns the biggest chain in the region. Mr. Hart, one of the men who 'believed in him', gives him a weekend guest card.

check.q: What happens on the raft, and what does Judy ask him at dinner?
check.a: Judy Jones roars up in a motor-boat, makes him drive it while she surfs behind, and asks him to dinner. On the sun-porch she says she has just been told a man she cared for is poor; then: 'Who are you, anyhow?' He says he is nobody — and that he is probably making more money than any man his age in the Northwest.

story.discuss: 'Let's start right. Who are you, anyhow?' — 'I'm nobody. My career is largely a matter of futures.' — 'Are you poor?' What is being bought and sold in this conversation?

story.title: Part 3 — The dream was gone

paras.to: That thing will come back no more."
skip: Dexter surrendered a part of himself
He was, as he found before the summer ended
The helpless part of trying to do anything about it
Early in their acquaintance it had seemed
in the clarity of the rising day.
The three days were interrupted by the arrival
On this note the summer ended
can what he did for her be understood.
When autumn had come and gone again
At the end of a week he went to a dance
should know more about such things.
He ceased to be an authority on her.
She had been away--he could have wept
In then, with a rustle of golden cloth
This story is not his biography
When, as Judy's head lay against his shoulder
the trouble to lie to him.
May one year back had been marked
He sat perfectly quiet, his nerves
Dexter waited with no apprehension of what was coming.

check.q: What does Dexter give up for Judy, and what does it get him?
check.a: Two years of his life, and then Irene Scheerer — sweet, honourable, engaged to him — whom he abandons the night Judy comes back in cloth of gold and says 'I wish you'd marry me'. Judy's interest lasts one month.

check.q: What does Devlin tell him in New York seven years later, and why does it destroy him?
check.a: That Judy is married to a man who drinks and runs around, stays home with her kids, and has 'faded' — 'she's all right', 'she has nice eyes'. Dexter realises the beauty he lost no longer exists anywhere, and that he can no longer feel anything about it: 'the dream was gone'.

story.discuss: 'He had thought that having nothing else to lose he was invulnerable at last — but he knew that he had just lost something more.' What is the thing he loses in that office? Is it Judy, or something in himself?

grammar.h2: The grammar this story runs on: regret and hindsight
grammar.intro: This is a story told from ten years later, by a man who cannot cry. Every paragraph looks back. English has a small, powerful set of structures for that backward look — and Dexter uses none of them, which is his tragedy. You will.
notes:
1. wish / if only + past perfect — regret about the past.
• "I wish I had taken the other job." • "If only we had left earlier!" (stronger, more emotional)
Never present tense after wish for a past regret: ✗ I wish I took.

2. should have / shouldn't have + past participle — criticism, with hindsight.
• "You should have told her." (you didn't) • "He shouldn't have quit." (he did)
• needn't have + p.p. = you did it, and it wasn't necessary: "She needn't have worn the gold dress."

3. Looking back with would rather / it's too late.
• "I would rather have stayed a caddy." (a preference about the past)
• "It's too late to go back now." / "It was too late for him to care."
These are the sentences Dexter cannot say. Notice how much they need a feeling to power them.

exercises.h3: wish and if only — put the verb in the past perfect
exercises.instruction: Complete each regret. Read it aloud as the character would say it — if they could.
items: Dexter wishes he ___ (never / hand in) his caddy badge that morning.
If only Judy ___ (tell) him honestly what she wanted!
Irene wishes Dexter ___ (not / drive) away with Judy that night in May.
If only he ___ (not / go) to the raft — he would still have his dreams.
He wishes Devlin ___ (keep) his mouth shut.

exercises.h3: should have, shouldn't have, needn't have
exercises.instruction: Choose the one the meaning needs. Careful: needn't have means it happened and was unnecessary.
items: Dexter ___ (tell) Judy about Irene in the car — but he couldn't.
He ___ (give) Judy two years; she gave him a month.
Judy ___ (wear) cloth of gold to win him back — a word would have done it.
Devlin ___ (say) 'she's all right' to a man who once loved her.
Dexter ___ (stay) a caddy — he was the best in the club.
answers: should have stayed (arguably — the story leaves it open)

exercises.h3: Put it together — the regret Dexter cannot feel
exercises.instruction: Fill each gap with the form the hint asks for. Then read it aloud as the speech Dexter would make if he could still cry.
items: I wish I ___ (wish / not / quit) that morning. I ___ (should / carry) her clubs and gone home and forgotten her. If only I ___ (if only / not / swim) out to that raft. I ___ (needn't / break) Irene's heart — Judy ___ (should / never / come) back at all. I ___ (would rather / stay) poor. But it ___ (be) too late for all of it, years ago.
answers: hadn't quit · should have carried · hadn't swum · needn't have broken · should never have come · would rather have stayed · was
exercises.note: Now say the last line of the story after it — 'I cannot cry. I cannot care.' — and notice what regret needs that Dexter no longer has.

grammar.outro: In the Speak tab you'll say the regrets the characters cannot — and decide whether Dexter's tragedy is what he lost or what he stopped being able to feel.

deeper.h2: Why this story stays with you
paras: Fitzgerald wrote 'Winter Dreams' in 1922, aged twenty-six, and called it 'a sort of first draft of the Gatsby idea': a poor boy from the provinces, a golden girl, money made fast, and a dream that survives everything except being fulfilled. The Minnesota lake is real — White Bear Lake, where the Fitzgeralds summered — and so is the caddy; Fitzgerald's own mother, like Dexter's, was the child of immigrants, and he never stopped feeling like a trespasser among the rich he wrote about.

The trick of the story is that Dexter gets everything. He is not defeated; he is 'so successful that there were no barriers too high for him'. What he loses is not Judy — he never had her — but the capacity to want, which was the only thing the winter dreams were ever made of. When Devlin says 'she's all right', the beauty that gave Dexter's whole life its direction is revealed to have been temporary, ordinary, and mostly imagined. Fitzgerald's last sentences are among the coldest in American fiction: a rich man on a lounge, crying for himself, because he cannot cry for anyone else.
deeper.note: Look again at the beginning. Dexter quits caddying the moment he sees Judy at eleven. He gives up thirty dollars a month rather than carry her bag. Is that pride, love, or the first winter dream — and is it the same thing he does with Irene fifteen years later?
questions: Judy Jones: villain, victim of her own beauty, or simply a force of nature the story refuses to judge? Find the line where Fitzgerald comes closest to blaming her — and the line where he refuses.
Dexter says he wants 'the glittering things themselves', not the glittering people. Then he wants Judy. Was he lying to himself, or is Judy a thing?
Irene is 'a curtain spread behind him, a hand moving among gleaming tea-cups'. Is Dexter cruel, honest, or both? What would a marriage to Irene have been?
'The gates were closed, the sun was gone down, and there was no beauty but the gray beauty of steel.' Is that maturity, or death? Would you rather be Dexter at fourteen or Dexter at thirty-two?

speak.useful: Hindsight: "He should have…", "If only she had…", "He needn't have…", "He would rather have…". Judgement: "What's striking is…", "You could argue that…", "On one level… but on another…".

tasks.label: Task A · Tell the whole story (4 minutes)
paras: Tell 'Winter Dreams' to someone who has never read it. Move through the arc: the caddy and the winter → the eleven-year-old with the golf club → the laundries → the raft and the motor-boat → 'Who are you?' → two years of Judy → Irene → the night in May → New York, Devlin, 'she's all right'.

Use at least three regret structures to say what the characters should or shouldn't have done, and at least five key words (melancholy, trespasser, petulance, indignity, unprincipled, invulnerable, incorrigible, glittering, surfeit, illusion).

tasks.label: Task B · The case for Judy (4 minutes)
paras: Everyone blames Judy Jones. Defend her: she is twenty, beautiful, surrounded by men who want to own her, and honest about it — 'I don't know what's the matter with me'. Then prosecute her for one minute: the picnic, the yawning, 'I'd like to marry you if you'll have me', the month.

tasks.label: Task C · Getting what you wanted (4 minutes)
paras: Tell a story — real, famous or invented — about someone who got exactly what they dreamed of and found it empty, or found they could no longer feel it. Use regret and hindsight structures to say what they should have done differently — or whether anything would have helped.
menu: A footballer who reached the top club and stopped enjoying the game.
A migrant who worked twenty years for a house in the old country and found nobody left to live in it.
Gatsby, Citizen Kane, or any story where the mansion is the loneliest place in it.
A musician whose first album was the dream and whose fifth is a job.
Someone who married the person everyone wanted — and then met the person.
A promotion that finally came, and the evening after it.

final: Dexter cries 'for himself now'. Is that the saddest line in the story, or the most honest?
Would Dexter have been happier as a caddy? Would you have quit that morning?
Is there something you want that you would rather never get, in case it turns out to be 'all right'?
Before you go — from memory: one sentence with wish + past perfect, one with should have, one with needn't have — each about a different character.
